title: Build a Web API with Flask
intro: **Flask** is a small framework for building web apps and APIs. You create an `app`, attach functions to URLs with `@app.route`, and return data — a dictionary becomes JSON. Code here can't run a web server, so these exercises use a practice copy of Flask and its **test client**, which sends requests straight to your app. The code is the same as with the real Flask (`pip install flask`, then `flask --app yourfile run`).

questions.prompt: `app.test_client()` lets you call your API without a browser — it's how real Flask apps are tested too.
questions.explanation: `<name>` in the URL becomes an argument to your function.

questions.prompt: Create `app` with a route `/status` that returns the JSON `{"ok": true, "version": 1}`.
questions.starterCode:
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

tests.name: json
tests.code:
r = app.test_client().get('/status')
assert r.status_code == 200 and r.get_json() == {'ok': True, 'version': 1}, 'GET /status should return the JSON {"ok": true, "version": 1}.'

questions.hint: Decorate a function with `@app.route("/status")` and return a dictionary.
questions.explanation: Returning a dict is the shortcut for `jsonify(...)`: Flask turns it into a JSON response.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method should an API use to **create** a new item?
questions.explanation: GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes.

questions.prompt: Using the `todos` list (defined for you), add `GET /todos` returning the whole list as JSON, and `GET /todos/<int:todo_id>` returning one todo — or `{"error": "not found"}` with status **404** if there's no such id.
questions.starterCode:
from flask import Flask, jsonify, request

app = Flask(__name__)
todos = [{"id": 1, "title": "Buy milk", "done": False}, {"id": 2, "title": "Call Ana", "done": True}]

tests.name: list
tests.code:
r = app.test_client().get('/todos')
assert r.status_code == 200 and [t['title'] for t in r.get_json()] == ['Buy milk', 'Call Ana'], 'GET /todos should return every todo.'

tests.name: one
tests.code:
r = app.test_client().get('/todos/2')
assert r.get_json() == {'id': 2, 'title': 'Call Ana', 'done': True}, 'GET /todos/2 should return todo 2.'

r = app.test_client().get('/todos/99')
assert r.status_code == 404 and r.get_json() == {'error': 'not found'}, 'A missing id should give 404 with an error message.'

questions.hint: `<int:todo_id>` turns that part of the URL into an int. Return a `(body, status)` tuple for the 404.
questions.explanation: Lists need `jsonify(...)`; dictionaries can be returned directly. A clear 404 tells API users exactly what went wrong.

questions.prompt: Posting a new message gives **405 Method Not Allowed**. Fix the route.
questions.starterCode:
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)
messages = []

@app.route("/messages")
def add_message():
    data = request.get_json()
    messages.append(data["text"])
    return {"count": len(messages)}, 201
questions.solution:
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)
messages = []

@app.route("/messages", methods=["POST"])
def add_message():
    data = request.get_json()
    messages.append(data["text"])
    return {"count": len(messages)}, 201

tests.name: post
tests.code:
r = app.test_client().post('/messages', json={'text': 'hi'})
assert r.status_code == 201 and r.get_json() == {'count': 1}, 'POST /messages should add the message and return 201.'

questions.hint: Routes only accept GET unless you say otherwise.
questions.explanation: `methods=["POST"]` (or the shortcut `@app.post(...)`) opens the route to POST requests.

questions.prompt: Fill in the Flask function that turns a list into a JSON response.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert app.test_client().get('/colours').get_json() == ['red', 'green', 'blue'], 'GET /colours should return the list as JSON.'

questions.explanation: Dictionaries convert automatically, but lists need `jsonify`.

questions.prompt: Add `POST /todos` that creates a todo from the JSON body `{"title": ...}`. Give it the next id (one more than the largest) and `done: false`, and return it with status **201**. If `title` is missing or blank, return `{"error": "title is required"}` with status **400**.
questions.starterCode:
from flask import Flask, jsonify, request

app = Flask(__name__)
todos = [{"id": 1, "title": "Buy milk", "done": False}, {"id": 2, "title": "Call Ana", "done": True}]

tests.name: create
tests.code:
r = app.test_client().post('/todos', json={'title': ' Water plants '})
assert r.status_code == 201 and r.get_json() == {'id': 3, 'title': 'Water plants', 'done': False}, 'Create the todo with the next id and return 201.'
assert todos[-1]['title'] == 'Water plants', 'The new todo should be stored.'

tests.name: invalid
tests.code:
_n = len(todos)
for _body in [{}, {'title': '   '}]:
    r = app.test_client().post('/todos', json=_body)
    assert r.status_code == 400 and r.get_json() == {'error': 'title is required'}, 'Missing or blank titles should give 400.'
assert len(todos) == _n, 'Invalid requests must not add todos.'

questions.hint: `request.get_json()` gives the body as a dict. Validate first, then build and append the todo.
questions.explanation: Never trust input: check it and answer with a 400 and a clear message when it's wrong.

questions.prompt: Add `GET /search` that returns the todos whose title contains the query parameter `q` (ignoring case), and supports `?done=true` or `?done=false` to filter by status. With no parameters it returns everything.
questions.starterCode:
from flask import Flask, jsonify, request

app = Flask(__name__)
todos = [{"id": 1, "title": "Buy milk", "done": False}, {"id": 2, "title": "Call Ana", "done": True}]
todos.append({"id": 3, "title": "Buy stamps", "done": True})

tests.name: q
tests.code:
ids = lambda url: [t['id'] for t in app.test_client().get(url).get_json()]
assert ids('/search?q=buy') == [1, 3] and ids('/search') == [1, 2, 3], 'Filter by q, ignoring case; no q returns all.'

tests.name: done
tests.code:
ids = lambda url: [t['id'] for t in app.test_client().get(url).get_json()]
assert ids('/search?q=BUY&done=true') == [3] and ids('/search?done=false') == [1], 'Filter by done=true/false too.'

questions.hint: `request.args.get("q", "")` reads `?q=...`. Query values are always strings.
questions.explanation: Query parameters are the usual way to filter, sort and page through API results.

questions.prompt: Your API runs `return {"error": "not found"}` for a missing item but keeps the default status. What will clients see?

options.text: 200 OK — with an error message in the body

questions.explanation: Without a status, Flask sends 200. Programs check the status code first, so always return the right one.

questions.prompt: Put it together: build `app` with an in-memory `notes` dict. `POST /notes` stores `{"text": ...}` under the next id and returns `{"id": n}` with 201. `GET /notes/<int:note_id>` returns `{"id": n, "text": ...}` or 404 `{"error": "not found"}`. `DELETE /notes/<int:note_id>` removes it and returns `{"deleted": n}`, or the same 404.

tests.name: crud
tests.code:
c = app.test_client()
r1 = c.post('/notes', json={'text': 'first'})
r2 = c.post('/notes', json={'text': 'second'})
assert (r1.status_code, r1.get_json(), r2.get_json()) == (201, {'id': 1}, {'id': 2}), 'POST should return 201 and the new id.'
assert c.get('/notes/2').get_json() == {'id': 2, 'text': 'second'}, 'GET should return the note.'
assert c.delete('/notes/1').get_json() == {'deleted': 1}, 'DELETE should remove the note.'
r = c.get('/notes/1')
assert r.status_code == 404 and r.get_json() == {'error': 'not found'}, 'A deleted note should be 404.'
assert c.delete('/notes/7').status_code == 404, 'Deleting a missing note should be 404.'

questions.hint: One route for `POST /notes`; one route for `/notes/<int:note_id>` with `methods=["GET", "DELETE"]` that checks `request.method`.
questions.explanation: Create-read-delete over URLs like `/notes/<id>` is the REST pattern almost every web API follows.
